items.questionAndWhy: Do people process media statements supporting and opposing a violent movement differently, and what can response time reveal about those judgments?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers conducted two priming experiments in India using pro- and anti-Naxalite statements and measured response accuracy, response time, and agreement with the statements.
items.whatTheyFound: Anti-Naxalite statements were processed faster and more accurately; participants tended to agree with those statements and reject pro-Naxalite ones. These are laboratory responses to specific material, not observed attitude change or later political behavior.
items.whatItMeans: Framing and prior orientation can shape immediate information processing. The claim that slower responses reveal active ideological rejection is an interpretation, not a uniquely identified psychological mechanism; transfer to other conflicts is untested.
items.streamTitle: Anti-extremist statements were processed faster in two Indian priming experiments
items.streamSummary: Two experiments found faster, more accurate responses to anti-Naxalite than pro-Naxalite statements. Response speed and agreement do not establish persuasion or the mechanism behind the difference.
items.attribution: Kumar et al. — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications

items.questionAndWhy: Does an adolescent's neural response to peer rejection predict later mood or depression, and does that differ by current clinical state?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers measured EEG P3 responses to peer acceptance and rejection in 179 adolescents, then followed depressive symptoms and smartphone-reported daily mood for up to 12 months.
items.whatTheyFound: Adolescents with current depression showed stronger P3 responses to rejection than acceptance. The rejection-related difference predicted later symptom severity mainly within the current-depression subgroup (n=37), and lower average daily mood across the sample; key associations were modest and near conventional significance thresholds.
items.whatItMeans: Social rejection sensitivity is measurable and prospectively associated with outcomes, but this observational neural marker does not show that rejection responses cause depression or provide a validated screening instrument. The small current-depression subgroup needs replication.
items.streamTitle: Peer-rejection brain responses predicted some later mood outcomes in adolescents
items.streamSummary: EEG responses in 179 adolescents were associated with subsequent mood and, among 37 with current depression, symptom severity. This is prospective observational evidence, not causal identification.
items.attribution: Kim et al. — NPP—Digital Psychiatry and Neuroscience

items.questionAndWhy: Does sequential working memory require replaying each remembered item, or can the brain retain the sequence through a different representation?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers used human magnetoencephalography, dimensionality reduction, and multivariate decoding to compare sequential neural replay with low-dimensional position-specific neural representations during a memory task.
items.whatTheyFound: Memory representations occupied distinct, behaviorally relevant neural subspaces by item position. The researchers found no detectable sequential replay during retention, supporting the subspace account within the sensitivity of their measurements.
items.whatItMeans: A null result for detectable replay constrains one memory theory without proving replay never occurs. The representation provides a concrete hypothesis for cognitive models, not a general-purpose decoder of thought.
items.streamTitle: Sequential working memory was represented in neural subspaces, without detectable replay
items.streamSummary: Human MEG decoding identified item-position-specific neural subspaces and no detectable sequential replay during retention. The null is bounded by the task and measurement methods.

items.questionAndWhy: Can sustained media-literacy instruction improve adolescents' ability to distinguish true from false information, and do effects extend beyond the classroom?
items.whatTheyDid: In a village-randomized field experiment across 583 villages in Bihar, India, researchers compared a 14-week, four-session misinformation curriculum with an English-learning control among about 13,600 adolescents, including follow-up and household measures.
items.whatTheyFound: The intervention improved measured discernment of health misinformation and source credibility. Some effects persisted four months later, extended to political-news discernment, and were also observed among parents; effects on behavioral measures were more limited and differed across subgroups.
items.whatItMeans: This unusually large field test supports sustained education as a candidate cognitive-security intervention rather than a single warning. It was first published in 2025, uses a bundled curriculum in one setting, and does not establish which lesson caused the improvements or effects on real-world sharing at scale.
items.streamTitle: Village-randomized media-literacy lessons improved misinformation discernment
items.streamSummary: A 583-village experiment involving roughly 13,600 Indian adolescents found improved health-news discernment, some four-month persistence, transfer to political news, and parent spillovers. The multi-part curriculum limits mechanism attribution.
items.attribution: Amar et al. — American Political Science Review (foundational 2025 field experiment)

items.questionAndWhy: How could fabricated political polls enter trusted news and forecasting systems, and how could their provenance be checked?
items.whatTheyDid: Polling analysts at FiftyPlusOne investigated anomalously clean respondent data attributed to Wedgewood Polls, compared metadata and sampling patterns with an independently commissioned reference poll, and asked the firm to explain discrepancies.
items.whatTheyFound: On October 20, Wedgewood publicly admitted fabricating its polling data. Multiple outlets and aggregators subsequently removed its surveys; removal counts differ across organizations. Reported campaign consequences and the firm's claimed motive were not independently established.
items.whatItMeans: This is an observed information-integrity failure in the evidence supply chain, not an experiment demonstrating voter persuasion. Source authentication, raw-data metadata checks, and correction propagation matter for intelligence and public-opinion assessment.
items.streamTitle: Fabricated election polling entered major aggregation pipelines before being exposed
items.streamSummary: FiftyPlusOne identified anomalies in Wedgewood survey data, and the firm admitted fabrication on October 20. Aggregators withdrew polls, but downstream effects on voters or campaigns are not established.
items.attribution: Radcliffe, Morris and Burton — FiftyPlusOne original investigation

items.questionAndWhy: What information actually helps an AI persona predict a particular person's later decisions rather than merely resemble population averages?
items.whatTheyDid: A preprint used a two-wave panel of 845 U.S. adults measured on 14 behavioral biases, testing synthetic respondents given increasingly rich demographics, personality measures, cognitive scores, or earlier non-target survey answers.
items.whatTheyFound: Description-based personas recovered only 53–67% of human between-person variation and 7–12% of the human test–retest signal by an individual-level metric. Adding behavioral history restored aggregate variation and raised person-level signal to 28%, still far below the human benchmark.
items.whatItMeans: Behavioral histories were more informative than profile descriptions for the tested individual predictions. Synthetic-audience work should benchmark person-level fidelity and error distributions, not treat accurate group means as human-substitute validation.
items.streamTitle: Behavioral history helped AI personas, but individual prediction remained weak
items.streamSummary: In an 845-person two-wave panel, demographic and personality personas poorly predicted individual biases; adding earlier choices improved signal to 28% of human test–retest performance. Aggregate similarity overstated fidelity.

items.questionAndWhy: Do automated benchmarks agree on which language models are most persuasive, and what do their scores actually measure?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers adapted nine previously published automated persuasion evaluations to a shared setup and applied them to the same 15 language models, comparing rankings, refusals, and general capability.
items.whatTheyFound: Across eight reliable methods, mean rank agreement was weak (Spearman rho≈0.25); seven different models ranked first across the nine tests. Refusals on manipulation tasks and task definitions contributed to disagreement.
items.whatItMeans: A single AI persuasion score is not a validated measure of human belief change. Assess distinct tasks, refusal behavior, and human outcomes separately; this preprint compares automated proxies rather than conducting a new human persuasion experiment.
items.streamTitle: Nine AI persuasion evaluations disagreed substantially on model rankings
items.streamSummary: Across 15 models, adapted automated persuasion benchmarks showed weak mean rank agreement (rho≈0.25). Differences in task definitions and model refusals limit broad persuasiveness claims.
items.attribution: Dementaviciute, Vaitonyte and De Bie — arXiv preprint

items.questionAndWhy: Can changing network connections be captured in a general evolutionary-game framework, and which network dynamics favor cooperative strategies?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers derived a structure-coefficient theorem for games on networks with exogenous Markovian changes, then tested its implications through mathematical analysis and numerical simulations of cooperation, trust, altruism, and fairness games.
items.whatTheyFound: Under the specified assumptions, three coefficients captured effects of network structure, mutation, and update rules. Most sampled dynamic networks did not favor prosociality, but a class of changing core–periphery networks did in the tested models.
items.whatItMeans: Time-varying relationships can matter more than a single static influence map. Using this theorem in behavioral COA simulation would require validating its population, payoff, and network-transition assumptions against humans; modeled prosociality is not observed social change.
items.streamTitle: Dynamic-network theorem identified conditions favoring modeled cooperation
items.streamSummary: A new evolutionary-game theorem reduced network effects to three coefficients and found some changing core–periphery structures favored modeled prosociality. Exogenous network dynamics and no human validation bound the result.
items.attribution: Zhang et al. — Nature Computational Science

items.questionAndWhy: Can ordinary smartphone images produce useful 3D digital twins without specialized scanning equipment, and how does reconstruction degrade with scale?
items.whatTheyDid: An eCAADe conference study combined smartphone image capture, structure-from-motion, and Gaussian-splat reconstruction, then compared small, medium, and large built-environment reconstructions against drone-acquired LiDAR ground truth.
items.whatTheyFound: The workflow produced visually useful spatial models, but geometric completeness and accuracy deteriorated as object or site scale and unobserved coverage increased. Captured coverage was a substantial limiting factor.
items.whatItMeans: This is a concrete lower-cost scene-acquisition pathway for possible XR rehearsal, training, or spatial-analysis tools. Those uses were not evaluated here; photorealistic appearance should not be mistaken for spatial or behavioral simulation validity.
items.streamTitle: Phone-image Gaussian splatting enabled lower-cost digital twins with scale limits
items.streamSummary: An eCAADe study compared smartphone-based 3D reconstructions against drone LiDAR across scales. Quality depended strongly on image coverage; XR-training transfer remains untested.
items.attribution: Aman et al. — eCAADe 2026 conference paper
